justice: Both sides of the road have paved sidewalks and a marked crosswalk, showing that some space is allocated to pedestrians rather than only to cars.
The corridor is very wide and vehicle-oriented, while no dedicated bicycle lane is visible, so street space is not distributed evenly across all road users.
Traffic rules appear clearly standardized through the overhead signal structure, speed-limit sign, and prohibition sign, which supports procedural fairness for users.
Accessibility is only moderate because curb ramps or flush crossings are not clearly visible at the crosswalk edges, and no tactile paving for visually impaired users can be identified.
safety: A marked zebra crossing is present at the intersection, giving pedestrians a formal crossing point.
The overhead signal gantry, countdown display, and 40 km/h speed-limit sign indicate active traffic control that can reduce crash risk.
The road is wide, smooth, and has clear lane markings, which helps drivers maintain lane discipline and visibility.
Safety is reduced by the broad carriageway and long crossing distance, which can expose pedestrians and cyclists to moving vehicles for more time.
No physically protected bike lane is visible, so cyclists would likely mix with motor traffic or ride near the curb.
livability: The street edges are dominated by open green fields and a blank wall rather than shops, homes, or active frontages, so everyday street life appears limited.
There are very few visible people or social activities, which suggests low immediate street vitality.
The sidewalks are clean and orderly, which contributes positively to basic environmental quality.
Regular street trees add some amenity, but the corridor still feels more like a pass-through road than a socially engaging public street.
sustainability: Street trees and large green verges provide some ecological value and can support carbon absorption and stormwater benefits.
The presence of sidewalks supports non-motorized travel to some extent instead of relying exclusively on cars.
No dedicated cycling infrastructure is visible, limiting support for low-carbon bicycle travel.
The very wide asphalt roadway and low-density roadside land use indicate a car-oriented spatial pattern with relatively high land and pavement consumption.
aesthetics: The street appears very clean, with new asphalt, tidy sidewalks, and well-maintained roadside space.
Rows of trees and open sky create a visually pleasant and uncluttered landscape.
The large overhead sign structure and consistent road furniture give the corridor a modern, organized appearance.
Aesthetic richness is somewhat limited because the surroundings are sparse, with few buildings, storefronts, or detailed street-edge elements.
comfort: Young street trees are present, but their canopies provide only limited shade, so thermal comfort is weak under strong sun.
The sidewalks look wide, even, and well paved, which supports basic physical walking comfort.
No benches, shelters, or resting facilities are visible, reducing comfort for users who need to pause.
Low visible traffic volumes and open surroundings likely reduce crowding and noise, supporting psychological comfort.
The broad exposed roadway and minimal enclosure may make the space feel hot and somewhat exposed rather than cozy.
walkability: Continuous sidewalks on both sides and a marked zebra crossing provide the basic structure for walking.
The pedestrian realm appears unobstructed and smoothly paved, which supports straightforward walking movement.
Walkability is weakened by the long crossing span across a wide road and the absence of clearly visible curb ramps or tactile guidance.
The corridor has little active frontage, seating, or destination density, so it is less attractive for walking beyond simple passage.
Limited shade from small trees reduces walking comfort in hot weather.
bikeability: No dedicated or protected bike lane is visible along the roadway.
Cyclists would likely need to share space with motor vehicles on a relatively wide and fast-feeling road, which reduces perceived safety.
There are no visible bicycle symbols, colored cycle markings, or bicycle parking facilities to support cycling use.
The smooth pavement is beneficial for riding, but this advantage is outweighed by the lack of separation and cycling-specific design.
